issues.legal_issue: A statutory provision cannot be held unconstitutional on an equality challenge based on presumed facts when the challenger could have pleaded and proved those facts.
material_facts: The challengers alleged that a retrospective valuation rule discriminated between pending and completed assessments, but did not plead that completed assessments had taken rent restrictions into account.
The High Court presumed that the earlier assessments had taken those restrictions into account and invalidated the rule on that basis.
An affidavit for the respondents stated that the rent restrictions had not been considered in the earlier valuations, and no material contradicted that account.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in relying on a presumption about facts that could have been established by direct evidence; the challenged provision could not be invalidated on that assumed factual basis.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory provision is presumed constitutionally valid. A person challenging it under Article 14 must make the necessary factual averments and adduce material showing the alleged discrimination. It is hazardous to decide constitutional validity by presuming facts where direct evidence is available. Assessment Committee of the Metropolitan Borough of Poplar v Roberts, Gulam Ahmed Rogay v Bombay Municipality, and Corporation of Calcutta v Sm. Padma Devi were considered in relation to rent restrictions and valuation.

predicates.constitutional_equality_challenge: A party challenged the constitutional validity of a legal rule on the ground that it treated people unequally.
predicates.challenger_supplied_no_supporting_factua: The challenger did not plead or produce material supporting the factual claim on which the alleged unequal treatment depended.
predicates.challenged_facts_were_capable_of_direct_: The facts underlying the alleged unequal treatment could have been established by direct evidence.

issues.definition: When a party brings an equality challenge but supplies no evidence of facts that could be proved directly, the rule cannot be invalidated on assumed facts.

issues.legal_issue: Treating pending assessments as a class distinct from completed assessments is not, by itself, discriminatory under Article 14.
material_facts: The challenged rule applied to pending assessments, while assessments already completed fell outside its operation.
The assessments that remained pending were governed alike.
The earlier valuations had not taken the relevant rent restrictions into account, so the evidence did not show that pending cases received different treatment in fact.
issues.conclusion: The distinction between pending and completed cases was a reasonable classification and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification founded on an intelligible differentia with a rational relation to the statutory object; mathematical equality is not required, and fiscal legislation is allowed a wide range of classification. Pending proceedings may be treated as a class if those within the class are treated alike. The Court relied on Ram Krishna Dalmia v Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar, Khandige Shah Bhav v Agricultural Income-tax Officer, Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh v State of Vindhya Pradesh, Hathisingh Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v Union of India, and Jain Bros. v Union of India.

predicates.equality_challenge_to_pending_assessment: A party challenged an assessment rule on the ground that it applied differently to pending and completed cases.
predicates.pending_assessments_were_treated_alike: The rule applied uniformly to the assessments that remained pending.
predicates.completed_assessments_received_no_differ: The evidence did not show that completed assessments had received materially different treatment in fact.
predicates.pending_cases_had_distinct_procedural_st: The cases to which the rule applied were still pending, unlike cases whose assessments had already been completed.

issues.definition: A distinction between pending and completed assessments is not unconstitutional when pending cases are treated alike and either no actual differential treatment is shown or their pending status supplies a distinct procedural basis for classification.

issues.legal_issue: Different conservancy-tax rates may be set for different classes of property by reference to the total cost of conservancy services, rather than the cost of serving each class separately.
material_facts: The municipality fixed a general conservancy-tax rate and a higher rate for large industrial premises, including mills and factories.
The municipality stated that it estimated the total expenditure required for conservancy services and distributed the tax burden among property classes using broad estimates.
The disputed properties were commercial industrial premises, not premises eligible for the concessional treatment described for certain public-purpose, residential, charitable, or religious premises.
issues.conclusion: The municipality could set different rates by property class after estimating the total cost of conservancy services; the disputed higher rates were not invalid merely because the municipality had not separately calculated the service cost for each class.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 129(b) and 137 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, as amended, govern conservancy tax. The Corporation must ascertain the total expense for the services and purposes described in section 129(b), but, apart from the categories covered by section 137(2) and (3), need not calculate a separate service cost for every property class. Section 137(3)'s cost-based concessional rate applies to the cases in section 137(2), not to the large commercial premises covered by section 137(1). A broad, reasonable estimate is sufficient; arithmetical precision is not required.

rule.if: differential_conservancy_rate_assessment and properties_were_divided_into_classes and total_service_cost_was_reasonably_estimated and rates_were_set_to_meet_total_service_cost and not properties_were_in_special_cost_based_category

predicates.differential_conservancy_rate_assessment: A municipality fixed conservancy-tax rates for different classes of property.
predicates.properties_were_divided_into_classes: The municipality treated properties as belonging to different classes when allocating the conservancy-tax burden.
predicates.total_service_cost_was_reasonably_estima: The municipality made a broad, reasonable estimate of the total expense of providing the relevant conservancy services.
predicates.rates_were_set_to_meet_total_service_cos: The different rates were set with the aim of raising the amount needed for the total conservancy-service expense.
predicates.properties_were_in_special_cost_based_ca: The properties belonged to a category for which the applicable scheme required the tax to be fixed by reference to the cost or probable cost of service to those premises.

issues.definition: When a municipality reasonably estimates total conservancy-service costs and allocates that burden among property classes, different rates are valid unless the properties fall within a category requiring a premises-specific cost basis.

issues.legal_issue: The authority to set different conservancy-tax rates for property classes does not amount to excessive delegation when the tax is guided by total service costs and a safeguarded budget process.
material_facts: The rate-setting process was connected to the total expense of conservancy services.
The Commissioner prepared budget estimates and tax proposals; the Standing Committee considered them; and the Corporation considered and determined the rates.
The statutory process provided for review and consideration of the estimates and proposals before rates were set.
issues.conclusion: The authority to determine different rates for different property classes did not suffer from excessive delegation of legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 129(b) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, as amended, permits different conservancy-tax rates for different property classes. The Corporation's opinion is formed through the budget procedure in sections 95, 96, 99, and 100, with the related procedure under section 150 where applicable. The total conservancy-service expense and the procedural safeguards provide adequate guidance.

rule.if: challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting and tax_rates_were_guided_by_total_service_cost and commissioner_prepared_budget_proposals and standing_committee_reviewed_estimates and municipal_council_considered_estimates

predicates.challenge_to_delegated_tax_rate_setting: A party challenged the municipality's authority to determine tax rates for different property classes as an excessive delegation of legislative power.
predicates.tax_rates_were_guided_by_total_service_c: The rate-setting authority was guided by the total expense of providing the relevant services.
predicates.commissioner_prepared_budget_proposals: The municipal commissioner prepared budget estimates and proposals concerning taxation.
predicates.standing_committee_reviewed_estimates: A standing committee considered the budget estimates and taxation proposals.
predicates.municipal_council_considered_estimates: The municipal council considered the estimates before determining the rates.

issues.definition: Rate-setting authority is not excessively delegated when total service costs guide the rates and the estimates and proposals pass through the described municipal review and decision process.

issues.legal_issue: Requiring payment of the tax claimed before entertaining a tax appeal does not violate equality or nullify the right of appeal when the appellate judge may waive the payment for undue hardship.
material_facts: The ratepayers appealed assessments but did not deposit the amounts claimed, and the appeals were not entertained.
The law permitted the appellate judge to dispense with all or part of the deposit if it would cause undue hardship.
The challenge concerned the deposit condition and related appeal and recovery provisions.
issues.conclusion: The deposit condition was constitutionally valid and did not nullify the right of appeal or create an invidious distinction; the related appeal and recovery provisions were also valid.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 406(2)(e) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act, as amended, the claimed amount must be deposited before the relevant appeal is entertained, subject to the judge's discretion to waive all or part of the deposit for undue hardship. A statutory right of appeal may be subject to conditions that regulate its exercise, and a disadvantage resulting from a person's own default does not create an Article 14 classification. The validity of section 411(bb) and rule 42 depended on that of section 406(2)(e). The Court relied on Hannah Cohen v Beneficial Loan Corporation and referred to the condition for appeal under section 30 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922.

rule.if: challenge_to_tax_appeal_deposit_condition and tax_appeal_required_deposit and appellant_did_not_deposit_claimed_amount and judge_could_waive_deposit_for_undue_hardship and appellant_did_not_show_undue_hardship

predicates.challenge_to_tax_appeal_deposit_conditio: A party challenged a legal condition governing whether an appeal against a tax assessment could be entertained.
predicates.tax_appeal_required_deposit: The appeal process required the appellant to deposit the amount claimed before the appeal could be entertained.
predicates.appellant_did_not_deposit_claimed_amount: The appellant failed to deposit the amount claimed.
predicates.judge_could_waive_deposit_for_undue_hard: The appellate judge had discretion to dispense with all or part of the deposit if it would cause undue hardship.
predicates.appellant_did_not_show_undue_hardship: The appellant did not establish that making the deposit would cause undue hardship.

issues.definition: A tax-appeal deposit condition and related rules are constitutionally valid when the appellant defaults on the deposit, the judge can waive it for undue hardship, and that hardship is not shown.

issues.legal_issue: Underground strata are land for land-tax purposes, and a person actually occupying the strata for underground infrastructure may be liable as the occupier even without a contractual grant from the municipality.
material_facts: An electricity company laid underground supply lines beneath streets that vested in the municipality.
The company occupied the space taken up by the lines and their bedding.
The company relied on statutory authority to lay the lines, and there was no requirement that its occupation arise from an agreement with or consent from the municipality.
issues.conclusion: Land in Entry 49 of List II includes underground strata, and the company was in occupation of the space occupied by its supply lines and could be made liable as the actual occupier.
issues.legal_principle: Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule includes the surface and underground strata of land. Section 2(30) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporations Act defines land inclusively, and sections 129 and 139(1) provide for property tax and primary liability of the actual occupier. Section 12 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, authorises a licensee to open streets and lay supply lines but does not prevent the licensee from being an occupier for tax purposes. The Court relied on Electric Telegraph Co. v Salford Overseers, Mayor, Aldermen and Councillors of the City of Westminster v Southern Railway Company, Assessment Committee of the Holywell Union v Halkyn District Mines Drainage Co., Rex v Chelsea Waterworks Company, and Reg v West Middlesex Waterworks.

rule.if: land_tax_scope_dispute and underground_infrastructure_was_laid_in_subsurface and entity_actually_occupied_space_taken_by_infrastructure and property_tax_law_made_actual_occupier_primarily_liable and premises_vested_in_public_body

predicates.land_tax_scope_dispute: A dispute arose over whether property tax could apply to land beneath the surface and who was liable for it.
predicates.underground_infrastructure_was_laid_in_s: An entity laid infrastructure in space below the surface of land.
predicates.entity_actually_occupied_space_taken_by_: The entity occupied the underground space taken up by its infrastructure.
predicates.property_tax_law_made_actual_occupier_pr: The applicable property-tax scheme placed primary liability on the actual occupier of the premises.
predicates.premises_vested_in_public_body: The premises in which the underground space was located vested in a public body.

issues.definition: When an entity actually occupies underground space for infrastructure on premises vested in a public body, it can be liable as the occupier under a property-tax scheme that places primary liability on actual occupiers.
